Three Brazilian brothers, Orlando (1914 to 2002), Cláudio (1916 to 1998) and Leonardo (1918 to 1961), who explored central Brazil and spent their lives protecting its Indigenous peoples. Their work led to the Xingu Indigenous Park in 1961, the first large Indigenous reserve in South America.

In 1943 they joined the Roncador-Xingu Expedition, part of the government's "March to the West" to open the interior. Over years of cutting trails and airstrips they made first contact with many peoples, and saw how disease and settlers destroyed them.

The park took in upper Xingu peoples such as the Kamaiurá and Kalapalo. As roads and ranches advanced, the brothers moved threatened peoples into it: the Kayabí, the Ikpeng in 1967, and the Panará in 1975, after a highway cut through their land. Their model was copied across the continent, but moving peoples off their own land, even to save them, was also criticised.
